questions.q: List the three discussion prompts given in the "Talking about the text" section of the chapter.
questions.a: The three prompts are: (i) A single event may change the course of history of a nation. (ii) Reality is what is directly experienced through the senses. (iii) The methods of inquiry of history, science and philosophy are similar. A wrong answer that lists plot events or character names reveals the student has not located the actual discussion prompts in the textbook.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what "Reality is what is directly experienced through the senses" means in the context of Professor Gaitonde's experience.
questions.a: In the story, Gaitonde experiences an alternate world that feels completely real to his senses—he sees British buildings, reads history books, feels the audience's tomatoes—yet it contradicts the "real" world he comes from. This challenges the prompt by showing sensory experience alone cannot distinguish between parallel realities. A wrong answer that only defines the phrase philosophically without linking to Gaitonde's two-world experience shows lack of contextual comprehension.

questions.q: Using the PEEL structure, write a 2-minute speech arguing for or against: "A single event may change the course of history of a nation," using evidence from the Battle of Panipat in the story.
questions.a: Steps: 1. Point: State your position clearly (e.g., "I agree"). 2. Evidence: Cite the textual moment—the bullet missing Vishwasrao at Panipat. 3. Explanation: Analyze how this micro-event altered leadership morale, causing Maratha victory, East India Company's containment, and a democratic India without colonial slavery. 4. Link: Connect back to the prompt: "Thus, the Battle of Panipat exemplifies catastrophe theory—a tiny deviation creating a macro-bifurcation." A wrong answer lacking textual evidence or PEEL structure shows inability to apply the discussion framework.

questions.q: Compare the discussion prompt "The methods of inquiry of history, science and philosophy are similar" with Rajendra's explanation of catastrophe theory and quantum theory. Identify two similarities and one difference.
questions.a: Similarities: All three disciplines use evidence (historical documents, experimental data, logical premises), build theoretical models (catastrophe theory, quantum many-worlds), and seek explanatory coherence. Difference: Science uses mathematical formalism and repeatable experiments; history relies on fragmentary documents and interpretive narratives; philosophy uses conceptual analysis. A wrong answer claiming they are identical misses the epistemological nuance the story highlights.

questions.q: Judge which discussion prompt from the chapter is most relevant to today's world of "alternative facts" and "post-truth." Justify with an example.
questions.a: "Reality is what is directly experienced through the senses" is most relevant because social media algorithms create filter bubbles where each group's sensory experience (what they see/hear online) becomes their reality, making shared facts impossible—just as Gaitonde's two worlds were both sensorially real but mutually exclusive. A wrong answer that picks a prompt without a contemporary justification shows weak evaluative reasoning.

questions.q: Design a new discussion prompt for a group activity on "The Adventure" that combines catastrophe theory and the role of individual agency. Write the prompt and explain why it would generate deep discussion.
questions.a: Prompt: "If catastrophe theory suggests small changes can cause massive shifts, does individual agency matter in shaping history, or are we merely observers of bifurcations?" This combines the scientific framework (Rajendra's explanation) with philosophical debate (free will vs determinism) and textual evidence (Gaitonde's thoughts triggering his transition). A poor prompt would be closed-ended ("Did Gaitonde have agency?") or unrelated to the chapter's core concepts.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Speaking and Listening: Discussion Points refers to structured oral ______ activities where students engage in evidence-based group conversations on thematic prompts from the text, practicing turn-taking, argumentation, active listening, and synthesis of ideas.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're in a book club ______ a mind-bending story where a historian slips into an alternate reality because a bullet missed its target in 1761.
What is Speaking and Listening? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Speaking and Listening: Discussion Points refers to structured oral communication activities where students engage in evidence-based group conversations on thematic prompts from the text, practicing turn-taking, argumentation, active listening, and synthesis of ideas.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Speaking and Listening?
questions.a: Students think group discussion is just sharing opinions without evidence.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can participate in a group discussion on the chapter's themes, presenting arguments with textual evidence using the PEEL structure, responding to peers by paraphrasing and building on their points, and collaboratively reaching a nuanced conclusion.
